opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think one of the big problems in AI today is that we have different languages for different levels, and they don't talk to each other. At the bottom you have tensors and GPUs, which is what deep learning runs on. At the top you have symbolic knowledge: rules, relations, logical reasoning. Historically these lived in completely separate worlds. You'd write your neural network in PyTorch, and if you wanted reasoning you'd bolt on some separate symbolic system, and the interface between them was always a mess.

The key observation behind TensorLogic is that these aren't really different things. A logical rule, a Datalog rule for example, is essentially a tensor equation. A relation is just a sparse Boolean tensor. Joining two relations and projecting out a variable is exactly an Einstein summation: you multiply tensors along shared indices and sum over the ones that disappear. So once you see that, you realize you can have one construct, the tensor equation, that expresses both a convolution and a logical inference rule.

That's what lets you span multiple levels of description. At the lowest level, you can write the actual numerical operations, the matrix multiplies and nonlinearities, very concisely. At the next level up, you can write whole architectures, like transformers, MLPs, or graph neural networks, as a handful of equations. Above that, you can express knowledge, rules, and reasoning, and it's all in the same language with the same semantics. You don't have to switch paradigms when you move up or down.

And then there's what I think is the most interesting part. Because it's all one language, you can move continuously between the symbolic and the numeric. You can take your objects and embed them in a vector space, and the logical rules become reasoning in embedding space. With a temperature parameter, you can dial between purely deductive reasoning, where there are no hallucinations, and analogical, similarity-based reasoning, which is where deep learning gets its generalization power. So it's not just that the levels coexist. They're interconvertible, and learning can operate at all of them at once.

To me that's what a real language for AI should be. Physics has calculus, and you can describe things at whatever level of abstraction you need with the same mathematics. Computing has had languages like that for general programming. But AI hasn't had its own language, one where the natural things you want to say, from the neuron level to the knowledge level, are easy to say. That's what TensorLogic is trying to be.

r003.rationale: It calls TensorLogic a shared language for multiple levels, but does not characterize it as a meta-representation for constructing representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the reason is that if you look at what's happening in AI today, we have essentially two very different ways of representing knowledge, and they live at different levels. On one side you have symbolic AI, logic, programs, knowledge bases, where everything is discrete, compositional, and you can inspect it and reason with it. On the other side you have neural networks, where everything is continuous, distributed, embedded in vectors, and you learn it from data but you can't really read it. And the problem is that these two worlds don't talk to each other. People bolt them together, they do neurosymbolic systems where you have a neural module and a symbolic module and some interface between them, but that's a kludge. It's not a unification.

What TensorLogic is based on is the observation that these are actually the same thing. A logical rule, a Datalog rule, say, is a join followed by a projection. And when you write that down in the language of tensors, a join is a product of tensors, a projection is a sum over an index. So a logical rule is literally an Einstein summation, an einsum. And that's exactly the operation that neural networks are made of. A matrix multiplication is an einsum, attention is an einsum, convolution is an einsum. So you have one primitive, the tensor equation, and from it you get logic and you get neural networks, not as two things glued together but as two faces of the same thing.

Now, why does that give you multiple levels of description? Because the difference between the symbolic level and the neural level is really just what the indices of your tensors range over. If an index ranges over a set of discrete objects, people, cities, atoms in a knowledge base, and the tensor is Boolean, then you have logic. You have predicates and rules and you can do deduction. If the index ranges over the dimensions of an embedding space and the values are real, then you have a neural network, you have representations that are learned and distributed. And crucially, you can have both in the same program. You can have a predicate that's partly grounded in symbols and partly in embeddings. You can take a knowledge graph, embed it, reason over it in embedding space, and then come back to the symbols. The same equations describe the computation at the level of symbols and at the level of vectors, you just change what the indices mean.

And there's also a third level, which is the implementation level. Because once everything is tensor operations, it maps directly to a GPU, to the hardware. So you have the knowledge level, where you're talking about objects and relations and rules; the representation level, where you're talking about embeddings and weights; and the implementation level, where it's all just einsums running on parallel hardware. And in most systems those are three separate things with translations between them that lose information. In TensorLogic they're one language. You can move up and down between levels without leaving the formalism.

I think that's actually the key to the whole problem of making AI that is both learnable and reliable. Because what people want from large language models, and what they're not getting, is the ability to reason without hallucinating. And hallucination is fundamentally a problem of having only the continuous level and no grip on the discrete one. If you can express the same knowledge at both levels, and you can control, through something like a temperature parameter on the reasoning, how much you're doing strict deduction versus how much you're doing analogical generalization in embedding space, then you get the best of both. You get the fuzziness and the learning when you want it, and the rigor when you need it. That's what a language for multiple levels buys you.

astra-6.text:
Because the same system can be described at several levels, and we want to be able to move between those levels without changing languages. At one level, you might have vectors, matrices, and the numerical operations of a neural network. At another, you have objects, relations, and logical rules. TensorLogic gives you a common way to express both.

The key connection is that a relation can be represented as a tensor. For example, a binary relation can be represented as a matrix, where an entry tells you whether a particular pair of objects is related. Logical operations then have corresponding tensor operations. And you can generalize from Boolean entries to numerical values, which opens the door to weighted relations and learned representations.

But a common representation doesn't mean that every level becomes equally useful for every purpose. If I want to express a constraint, a logical rule might be the clearest description. If I want to learn features from data, a distributed representation might be more appropriate. The point is to let those descriptions coexist and interact. You can express the structure you know, learn the parts you don't know, and connect them within the same framework.

Because the same thing can be described at several different levels, and we want to be able to move between those levels without changing languages. At one level, you might have vectors and matrices and the numerical operations of a neural network. At another, you have objects, relations, and logical rules. TensorLogic gives you a common way to express both.

The key connection is that a relation can be represented as a tensor, and logical inference can be expressed through tensor operations. So the symbolic and numerical views become two ways of looking at the same computation. You can use a discrete representation where that makes sense and a continuous representation where that makes sense, and combine them.

That’s important because intelligence isn’t just operating at one level of representation. We perceive something, form concepts about it, reason about those concepts, and use that reasoning to guide what we perceive next. What I want is a language in which those levels can interact, rather than having a separate formalism for each one and then trying to glue them together.
